title: Of age
paragraphs: I cannot accept the way we set down the length of our life for ourselves. I notice that the sages cut it back considerably from the common opinion. "What," said the younger Cato to those who would have stopped his hand from killing himself, "am I now of an age to be reproached that I am leaving the world too soon?" And yet he was only forty-eight. He thought that a ripe and advanced age, considering how few reach it. And those who, soothing themselves with I don't know what course of nature, promise themselves some years beyond that, might have some reason for it if they could be exempted from the endless number of accidents to which we are naturally exposed. What an idle notion it is to expect to die of a decay of strength — which is the effect of extreme old age — and to set ourselves no shorter span of life than that, when it is a kind of death rarer than any other and very seldom seen. We call only that a natural death — as if it were contrary to nature to see a man break his neck in a fall, drown in a shipwreck, be carried off by a pleurisy or a plague, and as if our ordinary condition did not expose us to these mishaps. Let us not flatter ourselves any longer with these fine words; we ought, perhaps, rather to call that natural which is general, common, and universal.

To die of old age is a death rare, extraordinary, and singular, and so much less natural than the others; it is the last and outermost sort of dying, and the more remote, the less to be hoped for. It is indeed the bourn beyond which we are not to pass, and which the law of nature has set as a limit not to be exceeded; but it is, also, a privilege she is rarely seen to grant us, that of lasting that long. It is a lease she signs only as a particular favour, and perhaps to only one man in the space of two or three generations, and even then with a pass to boot, to carry him through all the obstacles and difficulties she has strewn in the way of so long a course. And so my opinion is that once we have reached forty we should think of it as an age very few arrive at. Since men do not normally get that far, it is a sign we are already well advanced; and since we have gone past the usual bounds, which are the proper measure of life, we ought not to count on going much further. Having escaped so many precipices of death, into which we have seen so many other men fall, we should acknowledge that an extraordinary fortune like the one that has so far carried us through those high perils and kept us alive beyond the ordinary span of living is not likely to last long.

There is a fault in our very laws for upholding this error: they say a man is not capable of managing his own estate until he is twenty-five years old, when he will be hard pressed to manage his life that long. Augustus cut five years off the old Roman standard and declared that thirty was enough for a judge. Servius Tullius released the knights over forty-seven from the fatigues of war; Augustus released them at forty-five — though it seems a little unreasonable to me that men should be sent to the fireside until fifty-five or sixty. I would have our calling and employment extended as far as possible for the public good; and the fault, I think, is on the other side — they do not employ us early enough. This emperor was arbiter of the whole world at nineteen, and yet would have a man be thirty before he could be fit to settle a dispute about a gutter.

For my part I believe our souls are as adult at twenty as they are ever likely to be, and as capable then as ever. A soul that has not by then given clear evidence of its force and virtue will never come to proof afterwards. The natural qualities and virtues bring forth what they have of vigour and finesse within that span or never,
"Si l'espine rion picque quand nai, A pene que picque jamai,"
["If the thorn does not prick at birth, it will hardly ever prick at all."]
as they say in the Dauphiné.

Of all the great human actions I have ever heard or read of, of whatever kind, I have noticed, both in former ages and in our own, that more were performed before the age of thirty than after — and often within the very lives of the same men. May I not confidently point to those of Hannibal and his great rival Scipio? The better half of their lives they lived off the glory they had won in their youth: great men afterwards, true — in comparison with others; but by no means in comparison with themselves. As for my own case, I do certainly believe that since that age both my understanding and my constitution have rather decayed than improved, and gone back rather than forward. It is possible, with those who make the best use of their time, that knowledge and experience grow with their years; but vivacity, quickness, steadiness, and other pieces of us of much greater importance, and much more essentially our own, languish and decay:
"Ubi jam validis quassatum est viribus aevi Corpus, et obtusis ceciderunt viribus artus, Claudicat ingenium, delirat linguaque, mensque."
["Once the body is shaken by the violence of time, with blood and vigour ebbing away, the judgement halts, and tongue and mind dote." — Lucretius, iii. 452.]

Sometimes the body gives way to age first, sometimes the mind; and I have seen plenty whose brains weakened before either their legs or their stomach. And since it is a disease of no great pain to the sufferer, and of obscure symptoms, the danger is so much the greater. For this reason I complain of our laws — not that they keep us at our work too long, but that they put us to work too late. Considering the frailty of life and how many ordinary and natural rocks it is exposed to, we should not surrender so large a share of it to childhood, idleness, and apprenticeship.

[Which Cotton renders thus: "Birth, though noble, ought not to take up so large a vacancy, and so tedious a course of education." Florio (1613) makes the passage read as follows: "Methinks that, considering the weakness of our life, and seeing the infinite number of ordinary rocks and natural dangers it is subject to, we should not, as soon as we come into the world, allot so large a share of it to unprofitable wantonness in youth, ill-bred idleness, and slow-learning apprenticeship."]
